events.title: The death of Cnut the Great
events.shortBlurb: The Danish king of a North Sea empire, who had walked to Rome as a pilgrim and bargained there for his people, died at Shaftesbury…
body: Cnut, son of Sweyn Forkbeard, became king of England in 1016, of Denmark about 1018, and of Norway in 1028, ruling a broad North Sea realm. Though he had won it by the sword, he governed as a Christian king, bringing internal peace, repairing the churches his armies had once plundered, and endowing monasteries with lands and relics.

At Easter 1027 he journeyed to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II, and there, in the presence of Pope John XIX, he negotiated on behalf of his subjects: reduced tolls and safe passage for English and Danish pilgrims and merchants on the road to Rome, and relief from the heavy fees demanded of English archbishops when they came to receive the pallium. His letter of 1027, sent home from abroad, records these things in his own words.

He died on 12 November 1035 at Shaftesbury in Dorset — "on the second of the Ides of November," says the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle — and was buried in the Old Minster at Winchester. His empire did not long outlive him, dividing among his sons.
